seam_types: Plain seam with a zigzag or bound edge
fabric_card.pressing: High heat with plenty of steam, pressed while still slightly damp.
notes: Linen frays quickly and creases easily. Finish edges early.
Linen softens and shrinks with washing. Treat the fabric before cutting.
A lining stops linen from creasing too much at the seat or elbow.

prep: Linen frays quickly. Finish cut edges early and keep the pieces flat so they do not crease.
main_seams: Choose seams that enclose the raw edge (flat-fell, French or bound): linen frays and wears at the seam.
openings: Use interfacing of a similar weight, so stiff areas do not look out of place.
hem: A deeper hem looks good on linen and keeps the edge from fraying.
pressing: Press with plenty of steam while slightly damp. Press the right side through a cloth to avoid shine.

steps.title: Prepare the fabric
instructions: Check the care label or ask the seller how the fabric should be washed. Treat the fabric the way you will treat the finished garment.
Wash, soak or steam the fabric as that care says, then dry it flat or on a line.
Press it flat while it is still slightly damp, working along the lengthwise threads.
Fold it in half along the length and check that both cut edges meet and the fabric lies flat. If it twists, tug it gently on the diagonal until it sits straight.
Mark the right side with a small chalk cross or a safety pin if the two sides look alike.
tips: A fabric that will only ever be dry-cleaned should be steamed, not washed.
Save a small scrap from this prepared fabric: it is your test piece for stitches and pressing.
fabric_tips: Wash linen twice if you plan to wash the garment often. Press it before cutting.
steps.search_query: how to prepare fabric before cutting and stitching pre-shrink straighten grain

steps.title: Lay out and cut
instructions: Lay the fabric flat on a clean table, right sides together, with the lengthwise grain parallel to the table edge.
Place each pattern piece so its grain line runs along the lengthwise threads. Measure from the grain line to the selvedge at both ends to be sure.
Check that every piece fits before you cut anything, and that patterned or one-way fabric faces the same direction on every piece.
Pin only inside the seam allowance, or use weights, so the fabric does not shift.
Cut with long, steady strokes of sharp shears. Cut notches as small snips outward, not inward.
Keep the cut pieces flat and label each with a pin or chalk: front, back, sleeve, facing.
tips: Cut out curved edges slowly. A wobble in the cut line shows up in the finished seam.
Never cut anything that you have not checked against the measurements written for the tailor.
steps.search_query: how to lay out pattern and cut fabric grainline for beginners

steps.title: Mark the pattern on the fabric
steps.module_title: Mark the pattern on the fabric
instructions: Mark every dart point, pleat line, pocket spot and zip stop from the pattern onto the wrong side of the fabric.
Use tailor's chalk, a fading pen or tailor's tacks, whichever shows on your fabric but will not stain it.
For tailor's tacks, make a loose double stitch through pattern and both layers, then cut the loop and gently part the layers.
Match the notches of neighbouring pieces and number them with a pin or a clip so you can find pairs quickly.
tips: Test a marking pen on a scrap first. Some pens leave marks on silk that never wash out.
On sheer fabric use small thread tacks, so no chalk shows through.
steps.search_query: how to mark darts and pattern marks on fabric tailor tacks chalk

steps.title: Finish the raw edges
instructions: Decide the finish for each seam: overlock, zigzag, pinked edge or hand overcast. Fine fabric usually needs a narrow finish.
Finish the edges of every piece that will have an open seam, such as side seams and shoulders, before you sew them together.
Leave out the edges that will be enclosed, such as a seam that will be turned inside a French seam, or a hem that will be turned up.
Trim loose threads as you go and check that the finish did not stretch or ripple the edge.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: On sheer fabric choose a French seam or a rolled finish rather than a thick overlock.
fabric_tips: Finish all the cut edges soon after cutting, or linen will fray in your hands.
steps.search_query: how to finish raw edges seam finishes zigzag overlock pinking shears

steps.title: Sew a plain seam
steps.why: The main seams are plain seams.
instructions: Place the two pieces right sides together, edges level, notches matching.
Pin at right angles to the edge, with the pin heads toward the seam allowance so they can be pulled out as you sew.
Sew with the seam allowance that the pattern gives, keeping the edge of the fabric against the guide on the needle plate.
Backstitch a few stitches at the start and end, so the seam does not open.
Press the seam flat as sewn, to set the stitches, then press it open from the wrong side.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: Sew slowly across curves and at corners. A fast seam is a crooked seam.
Do not sew over pins. They bend needles and spoil the stitch.
steps.search_query: how to sew a straight seam on a sewing machine for beginners seam allowance backstitch

steps.title: Close the side seams
steps.why: The garment closes with side seams.
instructions: Place the matching front and back pieces right sides together. Match side notches, waist or hip marks and hem edges.
If a zip sits in the side seam, start and stop where the zip tape ends and leave that part open.
Pin the matching side-seam edges from the balance marks outward, leaving the pattern's openings free.
Sew the indicated side seams in the same direction on both sides, retaining any opening required by the pattern.
Try the garment on and check the fit. Take in or let out the seam as needed, then finish the edges.
Press the seams open, and clip the allowance at the waist so it lies flat.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: Baste first and try on. It takes minutes, and a changed seam costs hours.
steps.search_query: how to sew side seams and check fit on a dress or kurta

steps.title: Attach the waistband
instructions: Cut the waistband and interface one layer. Press the long edge of the other layer under by the seam allowance.
Gather or pleat the garment waist edge to fit the waistband, with extra at the closure for the overlap.
Sew the interfaced layer to the garment, right sides together, matching the centre marks and the side seams.
Press the seam up toward the band. Fold the band over so the right sides are together and sew the short ends.
Turn the band right side out, fold the pressed edge over the seam and pin it. Sew in the ditch (right in the seam) from the right side, or hand-stitch.
Add the hook and eye, button or other closing at the end of the band.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: Use a stiff waistband interfacing for trousers, and a softer one for a gathered lehenga skirt.
A drawstring (nada) needs a channel and a flat hole at the centre.
steps.search_query: how to attach a waistband to a skirt or trousers tutorial

steps.title: Sew a blind hem
steps.why: The hem is a blind hem, for a clean finish.
instructions: Finish the raw edge of the hem allowance, then turn it up along the marked fold line and press.
Pin or baste the hem in place, about a finger-width below the finished edge.
Fold the hem back against the garment so the finished edge shows. Take a tiny stitch in the garment, catching only one or two threads.
Take the next stitch in the hem allowance, a short distance along. Keep the thread loose. Repeat all around.
Press the hem lightly, from the wrong side, with a pressing cloth.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: A machine blind-hem foot works faster, but the hand method gives the softest result on silk.
Do not pull the thread tight. A tight stitch pulls a dimple into the right side.
steps.search_query: how to sew a blind hem by hand and by machine invisible hem

steps.title: Press the garment properly
instructions: Choose the heat from the fabric card, and test it on your scrap first.
Put a pressing cloth (a thin cotton or muslin cloth) over delicate fabric. Press with the iron, lift, move, and press again.
Press each seam from the wrong side, then open it up and press it flat. Press curves over a tailor's ham or a rolled towel.
Press the garment from the wrong side first. If the right side needs it, use a cloth.
Let the fabric cool and dry before you move it. Heat and steam set the shape only while the cloth cools.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: Never press over pins with plastic heads, or over zip pulls and buttons. They melt or leave marks.
steps.search_query: how to press seams and darts when sewing pressing vs ironing tutorial

steps.title: Final check and thread trimming
instructions: Trim every loose thread inside and outside the garment.
Check that every seam is closed and every button, hook or zip works smoothly.
Try the garment on, or hang it on a form, and look for pulling, gaping, twisting or a hem that is not level.
Check the measurements that the designer gave to the tailor against the finished garment.
Make a final press and hang or fold the garment as it will be stored.
preconditions: Complete: Mark the pattern on the fabric
tips: Keep the tailor sheet next to the garment. The final check is easier with the list in front of you.
steps.search_query: how to finish a sewn garment finishing touches trimming threads final check

Wash, soak or steam the fabric as that care says, then dry it flat or on a line. Press it flat while it is still slightly damp, working along the lengthwise threads. Fold it in half along the length and check that both cut edges meet and the fabric lies flat. If it twists, tug it gently on the diagonal until it sits straight. Mark the right side with a small chalk cross or a safety pin if the two sides look alike.
Scene 5 – Step 2: Lay out and cut: Lay the fabric flat on a clean table, right sides together, with the lengthwise grain parallel to the table edge. Place each pattern piece so its grain line runs along the lengthwise threads. Measure from the grain line to the selvedge at both ends to be sure. Check that every piece fits before you cut anything, and that patterned or one-way fabric faces the same direction on every piece. Pin only inside the seam allowance, or use weights, so the fabric does not shift. Cut with long, steady strokes of sharp shears. Cut notches as small snips outward, not inward. Keep the cut pieces flat and label each with a pin or chalk: front, back, sleeve, facing.
Scene 6 – Step 3: Mark the pattern on the fabric: Mark every dart point, pleat line, pocket spot and zip stop from the pattern onto the wrong side of the fabric. Use tailor's chalk, a fading pen or tailor's tacks, whichever shows on your fabric but will not stain it. For tailor's tacks, make a loose double stitch through pattern and both layers, then cut the loop and gently part the layers. Match the notches of neighbouring pieces and number them with a pin or a clip so you can find pairs quickly.
Scene 7 – Step 4: Finish the raw edges: Decide the finish for each seam: overlock, zigzag, pinked edge or hand overcast. Fine fabric usually needs a narrow finish. Finish the edges of every piece that will have an open seam, such as side seams and shoulders, before you sew them together. Leave out the edges that will be enclosed, such as a seam that will be turned inside a French seam, or a hem that will be turned up. Trim loose threads as you go and check that the finish did not stretch or ripple the edge.
Scene 8 – Step 5: Sew a plain seam: Place the two pieces right sides together, edges level, notches matching. Pin at right angles to the edge, with the pin heads toward the seam allowance so they can be pulled out as you sew. Sew with the seam allowance that the pattern gives, keeping the edge of the fabric against the guide on the needle plate. Backstitch a few stitches at the start and end, so the seam does not open. Press the seam flat as sewn, to set the stitches, then press it open from the wrong side.
Scene 9 – Step 6: Close the side seams: Place the matching front and back pieces right sides together. Match side notches, waist or hip marks and hem edges. If a zip sits in the side seam, start and stop where the zip tape ends and leave that part open. Pin the matching side-seam edges from the balance marks outward, leaving the pattern's openings free. Sew the indicated side seams in the same direction on both sides, retaining any opening required by the pattern. Try the garment on and check the fit. Take in or let out the seam as needed, then finish the edges. Press the seams open, and clip the allowance at the waist so it lies flat.
Scene 10 – Step 7: Attach the waistband: Cut the waistband and interface one layer. Press the long edge of the other layer under by the seam allowance. Gather or pleat the garment waist edge to fit the waistband, with extra at the closure for the overlap. Sew the interfaced layer to the garment, right sides together, matching the centre marks and the side seams. Press the seam up toward the band. Fold the band over so the right sides are together and sew the short ends. Turn the band right side out, fold the pressed edge over the seam and pin it. Sew in the ditch (right in the seam) from the right side, or hand-stitch. Add the hook and eye, button or other closing at the end of the band.
Scene 11 – Step 8: Sew a blind hem: Finish the raw edge of the hem allowance, then turn it up along the marked fold line and press. Pin or baste the hem in place, about a finger-width below the finished edge. Fold the hem back against the garment so the finished edge shows. Take a tiny stitch in the garment, catching only one or two threads. Take the next stitch in the hem allowance, a short distance along. Keep the thread loose. Repeat all around. Press the hem lightly, from the wrong side, with a pressing cloth.
Scene 12 – Step 9: Press the garment properly: Choose the heat from the fabric card, and test it on your scrap first. Put a pressing cloth (a thin cotton or muslin cloth) over delicate fabric. Press with the iron, lift, move, and press again. Press each seam from the wrong side, then open it up and press it flat. Press curves over a tailor's ham or a rolled towel. Press the garment from the wrong side first. If the right side needs it, use a cloth. Let the fabric cool and dry before you move it. Heat and steam set the shape only while the cloth cools.
Scene 13 – Step 10: Final check and thread trimming: Trim every loose thread inside and outside the garment. Check that every seam is closed and every button, hook or zip works smoothly. Try the garment on, or hang it on a form, and look for pulling, gaping, twisting or a hem that is not level. Check the measurements that the designer gave to the tailor against the finished garment. Make a final press and hang or fold the garment as it will be stored.
Scene 14 – Finishing and reveal: Give it a final press and a fitting. And here is the finished skirt.
